name: The anatomy of tyranny
plain_explanation: Aristotle gives an almost step-by-step manual for how a tyrant keeps power: eliminate anyone of outstanding merit, ban clubs, common meals, and education that might breed solidarity, keep subjects isolated and impoverished, use spies (including women and slaves as informers), and keep the people occupied and dependent through great public works or war.
precise_definition: Aristotle's description, in an 'ironically Machiavellian tone,' of the practical techniques by which a tyrant retains power: suppressing potential rivals, prohibiting associations and education likely to foster hostile solidarity, maintaining surveillance through informers, sowing internal discord, impoverishing subjects, and engaging in constant public works or war to keep the population occupied and dependent on a leader.
why_it_mattered: Russell calls this 'the one [passage], of the whole book, most appropriate to the present day' -- writing during the Second World War -- treating it as an uncanny anticipation of twentieth-century totalitarian technique, despite its twenty-three-century age.
historical_origin: Drawn from Aristotle's observation of actual historical tyrannies across the Greek world.
examples: The tyrant 'should employ spies, like the female detectives at Syracuse.'
He should 'make war, in order that his subjects may have something to do and be always in want of a leader.'
competing_positions: Aristotle notes an alternative, less brutal method of preserving tyranny, through moderation and outward piety, without deciding which method is more likely to succeed.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates, per Russell, techniques associated with twentieth-century fascist and totalitarian regimes.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The alternative, gentler survival strategy Aristotle mentions involves the tyrant 'seeming religious.'
